###### Abstract
We study one-dimensional screening when the Spence–Mirrlees condition fails along a monotone dividing curve, on which all types value marginal output equally. A single ratio, marginal distortion over marginal rent, governs the problem. When the relaxed solution stays in the positive region, non-decreasing optima in the positive single-crossing region are continuous if the ratio increases in the decision. When it crosses a flat curve and marginal rents are separable, every continuous contract is improved by a jump.
## 1 Introduction
Near the dividing curve the informational rent of every type is flat to second order in the decision, since v_(qθ)=0 there, while the virtual surplus is steep to first order. The object that measures this trade-off is the *distortion–rent ratio*, the loss of virtual surplus from raising the decision per unit of marginal rent created.
The weights of the measure are the distortion–rent ratio along the contract, and the conditions on them are conditions on the primitives.

# Monotone Allocations without Single-Crossing: When to Bunch and When to Jump
### Core claim
The central claim is that, for the class in which the dividing curve (the locus where every type values marginal output equally) and the relaxed solution are both strictly monotone, the optimal screening contract obeys a trichotomy read off the geometry of the two curves. When never meets , the optimum is continuous: it pools low types at a common quantity and then separates along a distorted branch (Theorem 1, under Assumption H on the distortion–rent ratio ).
### Load-bearing premise
The no-crossing result needs an extra condition on primitives — that the ratio of profit distortion to created rent rises as quantity increases above the relaxed solution — and also assumes the optimal contract stays above that relaxed solution; the paper leaves open whether continuity holds without it.
### A structured set of objections, weighed in public.
#### Referee Report
Under Assumptions 1–4 (constant-sign cross-derivatives, strict concavity of the virtual surplus), the relaxed solution q1 and the dividing curve are monotone, and the paper claims a trichotomy governed by how q1 meets q0: when they never meet, every optimal contract is continuous (Theorem 1); when q1 crosses a flat q0, a jump is unavoidable (Proposition
First, this is a serious paper: it repairs a known gap in Schottmüller 2015, provides the first proof of forced continuity under a primitive condition, and builds sufficiency certificates that settle cases where numerics are ambiguous. Second, the abstract's trichotomy oversells what is proved. The claim that a jump is impossible when the relaxed solution never meets the dividing curve is Theorem 1 under Assumption H (monotonicity of the distortion–rent ratio above q1) plus the restriction q≥q1.

# Maximizing Consumer Surplus Part II: Compromising
So it makes sense to study the mechanism that maximizes a weighted sum of profits and consumer’s surplus.   Standard optimal mechanism design proceeds by a sequence of mathematical tricks to derive a measure of a consumer’s value called *virtual surplus.*  Virtual surplus allows you to treat any selling mechanism you can imagine as if it worked like this
1. Consumers submit “bids”
2. Based on the bids received the seller computes the virtual surplus of each consumer.
3. The consumer with the highest virtual surplus is served.

If you write down the optimal mechanism design problem where the seller puts weight \alpha on profits and weight 1 - \alpha on consumer surplus, and you do all the integration by parts, you get this formula for virtual surplus.
For example, suppose the weight on profit \alpha is equal to 0 . That brings us back to yesterday’s problem of just maximizing consumer surplus. And our formula now tells us why complete rationing is optimal because it tells us that virtual surplus is just equal to the hazard rate which is typically monotonically decreasing. Intuitively here’s what the virtual surplus is telling us when we are trying to maximize consumer surplus.
Now back to the general case we are looking at today, we can consider other values of \alpha

We study one-dimensional screening when the Spence–Mirrlees condition fails along a monotone dividing curve, on which all types value marginal output equally. A single ratio, marginal distortion over marginal rent, governs the problem. When the relaxed solution stays in the positive region, non-decreasing optima in the positive single-crossing region are continuous if the ratio increases in the decision. When it crosses a flat curve and marginal rents are separable, every continuous contract is improved by a jump. When it crosses a strictly monotone curve, a contract that pools and jumps continues along the mirror of the pool if the ratio does not increase along it. Optimality among all implementable allocations, deterministic or random, is proved by a measure on the binding constraints whose weights are the same ratio; with constant curvatures and no crossing, it is also necessary.

...

The economic mechanism is the following. Near the dividing curve the informational rent of every type is flat to second order in the decision, since $v_{q\theta}=0$ there, while the virtual surplus is steep to first order. Bunching therefore appears from the erosion of rents near the curve, and not from a non-monotone relaxed solution as in the classical theory; and a jump across the curve costs almost nothing in rents and is strictly profitable. The object that measures this trade-off is the distortion–rent ratio, the loss of virtual surplus from raising the decision per unit of marginal rent created. Its monotonicity determines the shape of the optimal contract, within the class of non-decreasing contracts that stay on one side of the dividing curve when the curves do not meet; and its value along a contract is the weight that proves the contract optimal, without any restriction on the competitors.

The mathematical problem is to maximize the expected virtual surplus over the allocations that satisfy a continuum of global incentive constraints, one for each ordered pair of types.

### Background

The paper studies one-dimensional screening problems in which the Spence–Mirrlees condition fails along a monotone dividing curve. In the no-crossing configuration, the authors prove that any optimal implementable allocation is continuous when the relaxed allocation lies above the dividing curve and the distortion–rent ratio satisfies Assumption H.

The platform’s attention-allocation problem features network externalities. Attention allocated to creator exposure has a multiplier effect: greater exposure induces higher effort and improves content quality, attracting additional attention from interested viewers. This additional attention can be monetized through advertising or used to incentivize other creators, generating a feedback loop. The key to designing the attention allocation is to manage this attention-production loop by determining who watches whose content and how much advertisement, which creators receive subsidized exposure, how much, and from whom. To leverage network externalities, the platform may consequently direct viewers to content whose realized value falls below their attention cost. We call these distorted recommendations attention subsidies.
The optimal attention allocation follows a principle of network-effect-adjusted (virtual) surplus maximization. The surplus index captures both the direct monetization value of viewer attention and the indirect multiplier effects operating through the attention-production feedback loop. The optimal design uses discriminatory attention subsidies to shape the strength and scope of these network effects. The complementarity between viewer attention and creator effort generates an attention cliff: low-ability creators receive no attention, while those just above the inclusion threshold receive a strictly positive amount. The sources of subsidized exposure also vary with creator ability. Medium-ability creators receive subsidies within their own category, whereas sufficiently high-ability creators receive additional cross-category attention when the marginal return to effort is large. Moreover, the interaction of network externalities and private information generates local clustering of content quality among creators with different abilities.

Abstract

This paper analyzes product degradation as a screening tool under asymmetric information, emphasizing cost-efficiency over traditional concerns about information rents. We study a monopoly platform that sets meeting rates between buyers and two seller types — niche sellers whose high-quality good is valued by a fraction x of buyers and mass-market sellers whose good is valued by all. ConciseDetailed

## Core Idea¶

Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller actually receives for a unit and the minimum price the seller would have accepted — the seller's reservation price, which in competitive markets corresponds to marginal cost. For a single seller, surplus on any given unit is the gap between market price and the marginal cost of that unit; aggregated across all units sold, it is the area between the market price line and the upward-sloping supply curve up to the equilibrium quantity, geometrically a triangle in standard partial-equilibrium diagrams.

The concept does welfare-accounting work in microeconomics. Combined with consumer surplus (the analogous measure on the buyer side), it constitutes total surplus — the total welfare gain generated by a market transaction relative to the no-trade baseline. When policy distorts the market — a tax, a price ceiling, a tariff, a monopolist's markup — some of the initial total surplus is redistributed between buyers, sellers, and the government, and a remainder is destroyed altogether (the deadweight loss). Every standard welfare analysis of tax incidence, trade policy, monopoly pricing, and price regulation is a calculation of how producer and consumer surplus are split and how much is lost: a tariff that raises domestic price, for instance, increases producer surplus by the area between the old and new price lines and the supply curve, reduces consumer surplus by a larger amount, and generates deadweight loss in the triangles between the two.

## Why Trade-Policy Diagrams Need an Audit

Trade-policy welfare diagrams are easy to misread because several different things happen at once. A policy can change the domestic price, alter domestic production and consumption, and create a government receipt or a quota rent. These effects are not all welfare losses: some are transfers between groups within the country, while deadweight loss is the net loss from distorted production or consumption.

A reliable diagram audit therefore starts with the model and the price wedge, not with shaded areas. This tutorial uses the standard competitive, small-country setting: the country takes the world price as given, and there are no externalities or other market failures. Unless stated otherwise, amounts are domestic national welfare, and policy administration has no cost. In this setting, a transfer between domestic consumers, producers, and government changes who receives surplus but does not, by itself, destroy national welfare.

**Definition:** Consumer surplus (CS) is buyers’ willingness to pay minus what they pay; producer surplus (PS) is what sellers receive minus their willingness to sell for. A policy’s **deadweight loss (DWL)** is the positive magnitude of the net welfare lost because the policy moves production or consumption away from the efficient free-trade quantities. Government revenue and rents received by domestic license holders are transfers, not DWL by themselves.

Domestic quantity demanded falls, domestic quantity supplied rises, and imports equal quantity demanded minus quantity supplied at the domestic price. ultimate.title: When to Bunch and When to Jump
ultimate.snippet:
Our first contribution is the shape of the optimal contract in each regime, established as a matter of necessity rather than exhibited as a candidate. When the relaxed solution lies entirely in one single-crossing region, any optimal contract is continuous under an ex-ante condition on primitives — monotonicity of the distortion–rent ratio (Theorem 1). When the dividing curve is flat, the same variational argument runs in reverse: every continuous implementable contract is strictly dominated by one with a jump (Proposition 4.1). When the curve is strictly monotone and crossed by the relaxed solution, the shape of any contract that pools and jumps is pinned down completely: after the jump the contract follows the mirror of the pooled level — the unique decision generating the same marginal rent on the other side of the curve — until the relaxed solution overtakes it (Proposition 4.3). Whether the principal prefers that contract to the continuous candidate is a profit comparison, which the guiding application resolves in closed form.

webiq.title: Dual-Risk Theory Separates Market Discounting From Expectational Distortion
webiq.snippet:
Formally defined as the ratio of the fair finite-horizon present value under unbiased expectations to the biased present value calculated over the same observation window, the valuation ratio captures the proportional deviation between fair and belief-driven valuations. When expectations are completely unbiased, the valuation ratio equals exactly one, and the entire framework collapses cleanly into the standard discounted cash flow model. Conversely, when analysts or managers exhibit systematic optimism, the biased present value exceeds fair present value, driving the valuation ratio below one, whereas systemic pessimism yields a valuation ratio strictly greater than one.

By coupling the benchmark discount rate with the valuation ratio, the theory demonstrates that expectational distortion fundamentally breaks the classical equivalence between discounting and expected returns. Under biased expectations, an investor purchasing an asset based on distorted cash flow forecasts achieves an ex-ante expected return equal to the compounded benchmark rate multiplied by the valuation ratio. This analytical wedge gives rise to the gain of capital, a forward-looking structural measure of ex-ante alpha that quantifies the return differential attributable directly to systematic expectational distortion rather than stochastic market shocks. Calculated as the compounded benchmark factor multiplied by the valuation ratio minus one, the gain of capital isolates the expected excess return required to reconcile distorted investor expectations with underlying intrinsic fair value.

you.title: A Planet of Surplus Life: Building Worlds Beyond Capitalism - Shaw ...
you.snippet:
Capitalism is an immense machine for churning out surplus life. Its long war of enclosure has captured, controlled, and pauperised human life, and laid waste to nonhuman life. This paper argues that surplus populations—people rendered as economically redundant—are central to the future politics of our planet.
The goal for capitalism, of course, is for everybody to rent everything—even their own job. A world shaped by money but populated by the moneyless has existed since the outset of capitalism. And not just in the industrial heartlands. Colonial looting, slavery, and imperial wars are central to world capital, and have been since at least 1492. But the relationship between money and the moneyless has changed, particularly in dominant countries. Surplus populations typically provided a set of residual functions for capitalism: such as wage depression, an army of unemployed workers, and a disciplining effect on those who remain in the work force.
Writing at the apex of industrialising Britain in the 19th century, Marx viewed surplus populations as central to the motor engines of capital. Not an accident, not an aberration: surplus lives were produced by capital “in the direct ratio of its own energy and extent” (Marx 1990:782).
We start by exploring surplus populations and surplus geographies. This is followed by situating Marx’s ontology of economic bare life: the “virtual pauper”. We then provide our account of geographic justice and review work on post-capitalist geographies.
